text: There is a long running and, so far, inconclusive debate. <break time="0.8s" /> About what constitutes truth. <break time="0.8s" /> And how to represent that truth in writing. <break time="0.8s" /> A common misconception is that standard non fiction writing conveys facts which equate to reality. <break time="0.8s" /> Of course there is some truth in this. <break time="0.8s" /> But it is not the whole truth. <break time="0.8s" /> In fact it is impossible. <break time="0.8s" /> To use words to describe the whole truth of anything. <break time="0.8s" /> I can write a cup is on my desk. <break time="0.8s" /> And that is true. <break time="0.8s" /> There is a cup on my desk. <break time="0.8s" /> Even though you cannot see it. <break time="0.8s" /> You probably believe me. <break time="0.8s" /> Because a cup on a desk. <break time="0.8s" /> Is quite an ordinary sight. <break time="0.8s" /> But to tell the whole truth of that cup. <break time="0.8s" /> Would involve describing it in infinite detail. <break time="0.8s" /> Its colours and shapes, its history. <break time="0.8s" /> How it was made, by whom, from what. <break time="0.8s" /> Where those materials came from the number of times it has been used. <break time="0.8s" /> When, for what, and so on. <break time="0.8s" /> Writing can only communicate partial truth. <break time="0.8s" /> And writers make choices all the time. <break time="0.8s" /> About what to include and what to leave out.
